questions.topic: C Basics — The Main Application Function (main)
questions.q: Which code block serves as the main entry point where execution begins for any standard C program?
questions.hint: The name of this function is required in all executable C programs.
explanations: Correct! The `main()` function is the main entry point, and execution of a C program begins directly with it.
Incorrect. `#include` is a preprocessor directive used for including header files.
Incorrect. `stdio.h` is a standard input/output library header, not a function.
Incorrect. `printf()` is a library function used for printing text to the console.

questions.q: What is the default name of the created executable file if the `-o` flag is not specified when compiling with `gcc main.c`?
questions.hint: The file name dates back to UNIX origins (assembler output).
explanations: Correct! If you do not pass the `-o` flag, the GCC compiler saves the binary output as `a.out` (or `a.exe` on Windows).
Incorrect. The source file name is not automatically applied to the executable.
Incorrect. The compiler does not assign this default name.
Incorrect. The file `output.bin` is not created by default.

questions.q: Which GCC compiler flag is used to specify the output executable file name?
questions.hint: The flag consists of a single lowercase letter from the word 'output'.
explanations: Correct! The `-o <filename>` flag sets a custom name for the compiled executable file.
Incorrect. The `-out` flag does not exist in GCC.
Incorrect. The `-name` flag is used in the `find` utility, not in the GCC compiler.
Incorrect. GCC does not have an `-exe` flag.

questions.q: What type of computer memory is allocated for program variables during execution?
questions.hint: Fast, volatile, random-access memory.
explanations: Correct! When a program runs, variables are allocated in RAM on the stack or heap.
Incorrect. The hard drive stores the program file itself, not runtime variables.
Incorrect. The browser cache has no relation to a C application's memory.
Incorrect. External storage drives are used for persistent data storage.

questions.q: Which of the following data kinds are basic (primitive) types in C?
questions.hint: Types used for storing characters, integers, and real numbers.
explanations: Correct! `char`, `int`, and `float` are fundamental built-in C types.
Incorrect. `string` and `integer` do not exist as primitive keywords in C (strings are represented as `char` arrays).
Incorrect. The types `text`, `number`, and `decimal` do not exist in C.
Incorrect. `byte` and `boolean` did not exist in classic C89 (the `_Bool` type was introduced later in C99).

questions.q: Which rule is strictly followed when working with variables in C?
questions.hint: C is a statically typed language.
options: Every variable must be declared with a type before it can be used
Variables can be used without prior declaration
Variable type is inferred automatically upon assignment
Only numeric variables need to be declared
explanations: Correct! In C, the compiler requires explicit type declaration for all variables before use.
Incorrect. Undeclared variables cannot be used in C (this causes a compilation error).
Incorrect. Automatic type inference upon assignment is typical for dynamically typed languages.
Incorrect. Variables of all types must be declared.

questions.topic: Operators — Assignment and the x = x + 3 Expression
questions.q: What happens when executing the line of code `x = x + 3;` in a C program?
questions.hint: The right side of the expression is evaluated first, then written to the left variable.
options: The current value of `x + 3` is calculated and saved back into variable `x`
Equality between variable `x` and expression `x + 3` is checked
A compilation error occurs due to an algebraic contradiction
The value of `x` is reset to zero and then set to 3
explanations: Correct! The `=` operator evaluates the right-hand expression (`x + 3`) and assigns the result to variable `x` on the left.
Incorrect. The `==` operator is used to test equality.
Incorrect. In programming, this is a standard operation to update a variable's value.
Incorrect. The old value of `x` is not ignored; 3 is added to it.

questions.q: Which library header must be included via `#include` to use the `printf()` formatted output function?
questions.hint: The name stands for Standard Input / Output.
explanations: Correct! The `stdio.h` header contains declarations for I/O functions such as `printf` and `scanf`.
Incorrect. `stdlib.h` contains memory management (`malloc`), random number generation, and process control functions.
Incorrect. `math.h` contains mathematical functions (`sqrt`, `pow`).
Incorrect. `string.h` contains string processing functions (`strlen`, `strcpy`).

questions.q: Which format specifiers in `printf` output an integer, a floating-point number, and a single character, respectively?
questions.hint: %d — decimal/integer, %f — float, %c — char.
explanations: Correct! `%d` formats integers (`int`), `%f` formats floating-point numbers (`float`/`double`), and `%c` formats single characters (`char`).
Incorrect. `%s` is used for strings, and `%r` is not a standard C specifier.
Incorrect. Format specifiers consist of short letter codes.
Incorrect. Using `%d` for all types leads to improper byte interpretation.

questions.q: Which escape sequence is used to move the cursor to a new line when printing?
questions.hint: Represented by a backslash and the letter 'n' (newline).
explanations: Correct! `\n` represents a line feed / newline.
Incorrect. `\t` inserts a horizontal tab character.
Incorrect. `\b` performs a backspace.
Incorrect. `\\` prints a single backslash character.

questions.q: How do you print a double quote character inside a string literal like `printf("...");`?
questions.hint: Characters are escaped using a backslash.
explanations: Correct! The escaped character `\"` inserts a double quote inside a string without prematurely closing it.
Incorrect. `\\` outputs a backslash character.
Incorrect. `\'` escapes a single quote.
Incorrect. The sequence `\q` does not exist in C.

questions.q: What is the correct way to call `scanf` to read an integer from keyboard input into variable `var`?
questions.hint: The first argument is the format string, and the second is the target variable's address.
explanations: Correct! `scanf("%d", &var);` reads an integer and stores it at the address of variable `var`.
Incorrect. Omitting the ampersand `&` passes the variable's value instead of its address, causing a segfault.
Incorrect. The order of arguments is reversed.
Incorrect. There is no `input` function in the standard C library.

questions.q: Why is the `&` symbol placed before the variable name in `scanf("%d", &var);`?
questions.hint: The & operator returns a pointer to the memory location.
options: It passes the memory address to `scanf` so the function can store the input value there
It converts the input value into a string format
It checks whether the variable is empty
explanations: Correct! The `&` (address-of) operator passes the variable's memory address, giving `scanf` a target location to write data.
Incorrect. The `&` operator does not perform type conversion.
Incorrect. Checking values is performed using comparisons.
Incorrect. The addition operator is `+`.

questions.q: Which symbols designate single-line and multi-line comments in C source code?
questions.hint: Single-line comments start with two slashes, while multi-line comments are wrapped in slash-asterisk.
explanations: Correct! `//` creates a single-line comment (since C99), while `/* ... */` creates a multi-line comment block.
Incorrect. `#` is used in Python/Bash and C preprocessor directives, while `<!-- -->` is used in HTML.
Incorrect. The syntax is reversed.
Incorrect. `--` is used in SQL/Lua, while `{ }` defines code blocks in C.

questions.topic: Constants — Difference Between Constants and Variables
questions.q: What is the main difference between a constant and a variable in C?
questions.hint: Think about the names: constant (const) vs variable (var).
options: A constant's value cannot be changed after initialization, whereas a variable's value can change during execution
Constants occupy significantly more memory than variables
Variables can only be used for integers
Constants are stored on disk, while variables are stored only in RAM
explanations: Correct! Constants are declared as read-only entities; reassigning a value causes a compilation error.
Incorrect. Memory size is determined by data type, not mutability status.
Incorrect. Variables can be of any type (`float`, `char`, `double`, etc.).
Incorrect. Both types of data are stored in RAM during execution.

questions.q: What is the correct syntax for declaring an immutable variable using the `const` qualifier?
questions.hint: The const qualifier is placed before the data type.
explanations: Correct! Writing `const int MAX = 100;` declares a constant integer.
Incorrect. `#define` is used for preprocessor macros, not `define`.
Incorrect. There is no `constant` keyword in C (`const` is used).
Incorrect. `static` sets storage duration and scope, while `==` performs comparison.

questions.q: How is a global symbolic constant declared using a preprocessor directive?
questions.hint: The directive starts with a hash, requires no data type, and ends without a semicolon.
explanations: Correct! The directive `#define BUFFER_SIZE 1024` replaces the substring `BUFFER_SIZE` with `1024` before compilation.
Incorrect. The `#const` directive does not exist.
Incorrect. `define` without a `#` is not a preprocessor directive.
Incorrect. `#include` is used solely to include header files.

questions.q: Which rule must the first character of a valid identifier (variable name) in C strictly satisfy?
questions.hint: An identifier cannot start with a digit.
options: It must be a Latin letter or an underscore `_`
It can be any digit from 0 to 9
It can be a special character ($, %, @)
It must be an uppercase letter
explanations: Correct! A variable name in C must start with a letter (`a-z`, `A-Z`) or an underscore `_`. Digits are allowed starting from the second character.
Incorrect. Starting a variable name with a digit is forbidden by syntax rules.
Incorrect. Special characters like `$`, `%`, `@` are not allowed in variable names.
Incorrect. The case of the first letter is not restricted; lowercase letters are allowed.

questions.q: What does Case Sensitivity mean in C?
questions.hint: Think about whether variables 'myVar' and 'myvar' refer to the same memory cell.
options: Lowercase and uppercase letters are distinguished (for instance, `count` and `Count` are two different variables)
All variable names are automatically converted to uppercase
The compiler ignores differences between characters and numbers
Identifiers can only be written in lowercase letters
explanations: Correct! C is case-sensitive, so `var`, `Var`, and `VAR` are three completely independent identifiers.
Incorrect. C does not convert characters to a unified case.
Incorrect. Differences are strictly taken into account by the compiler.
Incorrect. Letters of any case can be used.

questions.q: What is the primary restriction when choosing a variable name in C?
questions.hint: Language keywords (int, return, if, else) are reserved by the compiler.
options: The name must not match language keywords (for example, `int`, `return`, `double`, `if`)
The name cannot exceed 3 characters in length
The name cannot contain digits inside
The name must match the .c source file name
explanations: Correct! Reserved keywords in C syntax (such as `for`, `while`, `int`, `return`) cannot be used as variable names.
Incorrect. An identifier can be much longer (standards guarantee significance of the first 31 to 63 characters).
Incorrect. Digits are allowed inside and at the end of a name.
Incorrect. Variable names have no connection to source file names.

questions.topic: C I/O — Behavior of scanf with the %c Specifier
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the newline character '\n' in the stdin buffer after the first scanf call.
options: Variable `c` will receive the newline character `\n`, because `%c` does not skip whitespace characters unlike `%d`
The program will work correctly and store 'A' in variable `c`
The program will crash with a Segmentation Fault
The second `scanf` will ignore `\n` and wait for character 'A' to be typed
explanations: Correct! The `%d` specifier skips leading whitespace (spaces, newlines), while `%c` reads the very next character, including the trailing `\n` left in the buffer after pressing Enter.
Incorrect. Character `'A'` will not reach `c` because `scanf("%c", ...)` instantly reads the leftover `\n` in the buffer.
Incorrect. There is no addressing error; variable addresses passed are valid.
Incorrect. Skipping whitespace with `%c` only happens if a space is explicitly added beforehand in the format string: `scanf(" %c", &c);`.
